extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, translators of classical texts, and educated general readers interested in translation and moral writing
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical guidance for translating and presenting classical moral works (e.g., Marcus Aurelius) to modern readers, and for judging the moral/practical force of such writings. Emphasizes accessibility, fidelity to thought, and the inspirational power of moral prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration / joyful emotion in moral teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral action requires an inspiration, a joyful emotion, to make it perfect; mere sense of labour and sorrow may paralyse ordinary men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts Epictetus's cold rational handles with Jesus's warm injunctions: the distinction of Christian morality is that it 'propounds this maxim with an inspiration which wonderfully catches the hearer and makes him act upon it.' Anti-pattern: moral writing that is purely schematic or arid, which may convince the sage but leaves ordinary readers unable to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral writing should move readers to practice, not only argue
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a moral maxim lies less in closer reasoning or purer sincerity than in the power to fire the hearer to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Epictetus suggests rational grounds for forgiveness, but Jesus's warm reply 'fires his hearer to the practice of forgiveness' — translators/critics should evaluate moral texts on their practical inspirational force as well as logical quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat classics as living documents with modern applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient remains should be handled not as dead, dry learning but as documents with a side of modern applicability and living interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Long is praised for treating Marcus Aurelius and other remains as 'food for men' engaged in contemporary life. Translators and commentators should highlight and make clear the ways ancient texts speak to modern concerns rather than presenting them only as antiquarian artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity, substantiality, and precision in rendering thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator must aim for substantiality, soundness, and precision to seize the clear thought underlying dubious or corrupt original wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the original language is 'corrupt, almost always hard and obscure', accurate rendering of the clear underlying thought is essential. Example: Mr. Long 'firmly seized upon the clear thought' in a difficult Greek passage and rendered it distinctly. Scoring note: accuracy of conveyed thought outweighs literal prettiness when original is obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture and transmit the living spirit, not only literal words
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond fidelity, a good translation should preserve the living spirit — the warmth, tenderness, or force — which gives the original its peculiar character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translator should render Marcus Aurelius 'suffused and softened by something of this very sentiment' (Christian-like warmth). Anti-pattern: technically accurate but sterile translations that lose the author's emotional or moral tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and idiomatic plainness for a general public
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain, idiomatic, non‑professional language and familiar names/terms so the work is accessible to the general public rather than only to scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pedantic forms (e.g., 'Ethic and Dialectic' vs. 'Ethics and Dialectics') and obscure names ('Hellenes'/'Komans') where 'Greeks'/'Romans' will reach readers. Use familiar name-forms (call him 'Marcus Aurelius' not 'Marcus Antoninus') and translate currency/units into familiar equivalents ('pence' not 'denarii') to make the text live for ordinary readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer accessibility over punctilious scholarly manner when addressing lay readers
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating short masterpieces intended for the public, the aim should be popularity and currency rather than strict pedantic phraseology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translator's target audience matters: for a general readership render in language 'perfectly plain and unprofessional.' Anti-pattern: prioritizing minute scholastic accuracy at the expense of readability and modern applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone toward predecessors: restraint & generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator should deal leniently with predecessors and avoid unduly harsh or dismissive language about earlier translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Long's description of Jeremy Collier as 'a most coarse and vulgar copy' is criticized as unnecessarily hard. Courtesy and acknowledgment of predecessors' contributions (even with defects) is recommended as a matter of taste and gratitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve stylistic force, rhythm, and warmth where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an earlier or alternative rendering has 'warmth of feeling' or rhythmic impulse that conveys the original's power, a translator should not sacrifice that force for over-smoothness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative passages show Jeremy Collier's impetuosity and rhythm giving force that Mr. Long lacks; translators should aim to retain such qualities where they serve the author's effect. Anti-pattern: smoothing that removes vigor and immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seize clear thought even from crabbed or involved original prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When the author's language is crabbed or obscure, the translator's task is to discern the clear thought underneath and render it distinctly, sometimes at the cost of reproducing awkward surface phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mr. Long is praised for taking 'the clear thought which is certainly at the bottom of that troubled wording' and making it distinct while keeping an appropriate shade of difficulty. Scoring guidance: prioritize intelligibility of underlying meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translator's aim: make the author useful and edifying to modern life
rubrics_metrics.description: The translator should present the author as a present source 'from which to draw example of life, and instruction of manners' — i.e., emphasize practical lessons for contemporary readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Long's notes treat ancient figures 'not as food for schoolboys, but as food for men engaged in the current of contemporary life and action.' Translators should explicate practical relevance, not merely historical or philological detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral-writing practical rule: do nothing without a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical moral rule: 'Let nothing be done without a purpose' — remove unnecessary acts and unnecessary thoughts to gain leisure and reduce uneasiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus Aurelius's counsel is given as a rule for 'drive at practice': on every occasion ask 'Is this one of the unnecessary things?' and eliminate it. Application: critics and teachers should evaluate moral texts for clear, practicable precepts like this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral-writing discipline: check purposeless, curious, or malignant thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Train oneself to check thoughts that are without purpose, especially over-curious, malignant, envious, or suspicious thoughts; cultivate simplicity and benevolence of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marcus recommends one 'use himself to think of those things only about which... with perfect openness thou mightest immediately answer.' Evaluate moral prose by how well it inculcates this inward discipline and simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform good acts without counting or seeking recompense
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral ideal: do good as an end in itself — like a vine producing grapes — not to be paid or publicly credited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passage: 'A man when he has done a good act, does not call out for others to come and see, but he goes on to another act.' Moral writings should promote this internalized, non‑egotistical ethic; anti-pattern: exhortations that encourage seeking reward or public recognition for virtue.
